items.title: Score a market before you spend a year on it
items.excerpt: Pick a market on a hunch and you find out a year later whether it was right. Here are the six things worth scoring first, and the free public data that lets you check most of them yourself.
items.author: Scott Robinson
items.body:
Pick a market on a hunch and you find out whether it was right about a year later, after the flights, the trade show and the distributor agreement. That's an expensive way to learn something you could have checked in an afternoon.

I've spent 30 years in industrial sales and built three markets from zero. Seeing a market move early is the whole game, and it starts with knowing which market deserves the effort in the first place.

So score it first. The free [Market Read](https://parteloa.com/market-revenue-opportunity.html) scores a product in any market on six dimensions: product and market fit, buyer fit, competitive position, market access, commercial readiness and market opportunity. It's 11 questions, takes a few minutes and names the one thing standing between you and the revenue.

You don't have to take a score on trust, though. For most of those six there's public data you can check yourself.

## Is there demand you can actually see?

Market opportunity and product fit start with a simple question. Does the country buy what you make?

[UN Comtrade](https://comtradeplus.un.org/) publishes annual and monthly imports and exports by product and trading partner, reported to the United Nations by about 200 countries and areas and put on common classifications so you can compare them. The numbers are reported by national authorities rather than estimated.

Find your product code, pull the imports for the country you're weighing up and look at who supplies it. Flat imports tell you one thing. One supplier country taking most of the volume tells you something about competitive position as well.

What it won't tell you is who the buyers are or how they buy. Import data is a demand signal, not a customer list.

## Who's buying, and how do they buy?

Buyer fit and market access are where a lot of market plans fall over. A big import number doesn't help much if the buyers are public bodies buying through tenders you've never seen.

If public buyers matter in your sector, read the procurement record. In Europe that's [TED](https://ted.europa.eu/en/about-ted), the online version of the Supplement to the Official Journal of the EU. More than 3,000 public procurement notices are published there every weekday, and you can browse, search and sort them by country, region and business sector.

Search your sector in the country you're scoring. The notices show you who buys, how often and what they ask for, which is a far better read on access than a sector report.

## Who's already there?

Competitive position and your route in both come down to names. The competitors you'll meet, and the partners you might sign.

Company registers are where that starts. In the UK the register sits with [Companies House](https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/), and [GOV.UK](https://www.gov.uk/get-information-about-a-company) sets out what you can get for free: registered address and date of incorporation, current and resigned officers, document images and insolvency information. You can also set up free email alerts that tell you when a company updates its details, such as a change of director.

Run the competitors through it. Run any partner on the shortlist through it before you sign anything. A register won't tell you whether someone's good at selling, and [Companies House itself says](https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/) it doesn't check the accuracy of the information filed. Treat it as a starting point, not a verdict.

## Commercial readiness is the one you score yourself

There's no public dataset for this one. It's whether your business can actually serve the market: the price, the approvals, the stock, the people and the time to follow it through. Be honest here. A good market opened by a team that wasn't ready still looks like a bad market a year later.

Here's a plainly hypothetical example. A test equipment maker is weighing up a European market. Say the imports for its product code are steady and spread across several supplier countries, and TED shows regular notices from public labs in its sector. That's a market worth a closer look. Say instead the imports are tiny and TED shows almost nothing in its sector. That's one to park, and it's cost an afternoon, not a year.

## The short version

- Score a market on six dimensions before you spend on it, not on a hunch.
- Trade statistics show demand. They don't show buyers.
- Procurement notices show who buys and how, if public buyers matter in your sector.
- Company registers show who you'll compete with and who you'd be signing.
- Commercial readiness is on you, so score it honestly.

Run the Market Read on the market you're weighing up now. Then [start free](https://app.parteloa.com/?mode=signup) and Parteloa can watch the companies, territories and projects in it and tell you when something moves.

## Sources

- United Nations, "UN Comtrade Database", 2026. https://comtradeplus.un.org/
- Publications Office of the European Union, "About TED", 2026. https://ted.europa.eu/en/about-ted
- GOV.UK, "Get information about a company", 2026. https://www.gov.uk/get-information-about-a-company
- Companies House, "Find and update company information", 2026. https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/
